books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: John Brown, note written on the morning of his execution, December 2, 1859. Public domain.
stimulus.text: I, John Brown, am now quite certain that the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood. I had, as I now think, vainly flattered myself that without very much bloodshed it might be done.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Brown’s raid most directly deepened the sectional conflict because Southerners took it as proof that

options.text: Northern abolitionists meant to destroy slavery by violence.
the Republican Party had already won the presidency.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the raid came in 1859, a year before Lincoln’s election; no Republican had yet won the White House.

options.text: the Supreme Court supported slave rebellions.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the Court had ruled for slavery in Dred Scott in 1857; no court backed Brown’s raid.

options.text: most Northerners approved of armed rebellion.
options.misconception: Background from the books: most Northern politicians condemned the raid; the South’s fear was of a conspiracy, not of a Northern majority.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Brown’s ties to leading abolitionists let Southerners read one man’s raid as a Northern plot, and that reading, more than the raid itself, broke trust.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the raid came in 1859, a year before Lincoln’s election; no Republican had yet won the White House.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the Court had ruled for slavery in Dred Scott in 1857; no court backed Brown’s raid.
rationales.D: Background from the books: most Northern politicians condemned the raid; the South’s fear was of a conspiracy, not of a Northern majority.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what Southerners saw: a Northern abolitionist seizing a federal armory to arm the enslaved.
2. Background from the books: Brown knew leading abolitionists, including Frederick Douglass, and the South read the raid as their plot.
3. Weigh the truth against the fear: most Northern politicians condemned Brown, but the South believed the conspiracy.
Remember: in a sectional crisis, what one side believes the other meant can matter more than what happened.
